people with HCU, mental health and/or substance use problems can achieve the same outcomes as those without these co morbidities if they have access to the same level of care and support.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is clear and compelling that people with mental health and/or substance use co-morbidity should have equal access to HCV antiviral therapy.
people with HVC, mental health and/or substance use co-morbidity have similar outcomes to those without co-morbid conditions.
people with HVC, mental health and drug and alcohol co-morbid disorders have similar access and outcomes to antiviral treatment as people without these co-morbidity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the exclusion of people with mental health and/or substance use problems from HCV antiviral treatment is no longer justified and is contrary to current evidence.
the evidence supports the inclusion of HCV patients with mental health co-morbid conditions to antiviral treatment and that this should be considered in a primary health care setting.

the evidence base for increased access to interferons by people with HVC, mental health and/or substance use co-morbidity is now substantial, but that the implementation of this evidence in clinical practice is still limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people with HVC, mental health and/or substance use disorders can be safely and effectively treated with interferon.
people with HVC, mental health and co-occurring substance use disorders can be safely treated and have similar clinical outcomes as people without these co-morbities.

people with mental health and/or substance use disorders can benefit from treatment for HCV, but that there are many barriers that must be addressed to increase equitable access to HCV antiviral therapy.
